title: Rivet and Ferry: grace that makes pleasing is God's favour itself
source_text: XV. Rivetus autem in summa controversiarum tractatu quarto quaestione secunda, per gratiam gratis datam intelligit omnia dona gratiae; per gratiam vero gratum facientem, quam etiam gratis dantem vocat, intelligi vult ipsum Dei favorem, a quo dona illa procedunt. Quo sensu Paulus Ferrius in specimine Scholastici orthodoxi capite trigesimo, distinctionem eandem usurpat. Nam per gratiam gratum facientem significat gratiam Deo immanentem, quae non ponit aliquid circa gratificatum, sed est ipse Dei amor: sub gratia vero gratis data comprehendit omnia beneficia vocationis, justificationis, &c. ex gratia gratis dante, tanquam ex fonte uberrimo in nos dimanantia.
pass_a_gloss: XV. But Rivet in the summary of controversies tractate four question two, by grace freely given understands all the gifts of grace; but by grace making pleasing, which he also calls freely giving, he will have understood the very favour of God, from which those gifts proceed. In which sense Paul Ferry in the specimen of the orthodox Scholastic chapter thirty, uses the same distinction. For by grace making pleasing he signifies grace immanent in God, which does not posit anything about the one favoured, but is the very love of God: but under grace freely given he comprehends all the benefits of calling, justification, &c. flowing down upon us from grace freely giving, as from a most abundant fountain.
pass_b_english: Thesis XV. Rivet, however, in his Summary of Controversies (tractate 4, question 2), takes grace freely given to mean all the gifts of grace. By grace that makes pleasing, which he also calls grace that gives freely, he means God's favour itself, from which those gifts come.

Paul Ferry uses the same distinction in this sense in chapter 30 of his Specimen of an Orthodox Scholastic. By grace that makes pleasing he means grace that remains within God, which places nothing in the one who is favoured but is simply God's love. Under grace freely given he includes all the benefits of calling, justification and so on, which flow down to us from the grace that gives freely as from an overflowing spring.

choices.why: The scholastic pair (Aquinas, Summa theologiae I-II q. 111 a. 1): gifts given for the good of others versus the grace that makes its bearer pleasing to God. Kept literal because the Reformed objections turn on the very words.
